claims.text: Chemical disorder in rare-earth-free transition-metal high-entropy alloys produces spatial variation in magnetic exchange energies.
An optimal degree of chemical disorder promotes a bimodal distribution of magnetic exchange interactions.
Nanoscale regions enriched in strongly ferromagnetically coupled atomic pairs coexist with a matrix of weaker or frustrated interactions.
Locally enhanced ferromagnetic clusters rapidly align under low applied magnetic fields.
Rapid low-field alignment of the ferromagnetic clusters produces a large magnetic entropy change.
The surrounding disordered matrix minimizes magnetic hysteresis.
The surrounding disordered matrix supports rapid thermal conduction and heat exchange.
The surrounding disordered matrix maintains mechanical integrity.
The proposed initial material is a single-phase, chemically disordered alloy composed exclusively of transition metals.
Compositional tuning and controlled heat treatment can alter the distribution of exchange interactions through changes in local chemical environments.
The proposed tuning can increase the proportion of strong ferromagnetic neighbor interactions while preserving overall chemical disorder.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the treated alloy will exhibit a significant increase in magnetic entropy change at low fields.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the treated alloy will exhibit reduced magnetic hysteresis.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the treated alloy will have unchanged or improved thermal conductivity and heat-exchange rate.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the treated alloy will maintain or improve mechanical stability.
The hypothesis is expected to apply near room temperature under magnetic fields of a few tesla or less and dynamic cycling.
The hypothesis is restricted to rare-earth-free, transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys that retain a single-phase disordered structure.

Absence of a statistically significant low-field entropy-change improvement together with maintained heat exchange and mechanical stability, or the occurrence of increased hysteresis, would falsify the hypothesis.
